questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Vancouver is a city located in close proximity to some of the most beautiful natural areas in the world. Mountains and temperate rainforests surround the region and are easily accessible compared to Copenhagen. Moreover, the province of British Columbia is a major global supplier of wood, which is why UBC possesses some of the most advanced forestry expertise.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
I would think that it always is a confusing time whenever one moves to a different country. However, i thought that the process was quite easy, based on the circumstances of being abroad. I was lucky enough to have accomodation through the campus, so i already knew when the dorm let me move in. Then it was just a matter of showing up at the designated time.

UBC sends out plenty information, way to much in my opnion. If you succesfully get through the application i would say you are more than capable of finding your way once you arrive.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: My dorm had a designated move-in day, so I knew when to arrive. I had volunteered to help on that day, which allowed me to move in a day earlier. The work was really easy. I mostly directed people and traffic along with a few others. Even though I didn’t know my way around campus, it was simple, trust me. I also got the chance to meet some other people during move-in, which was a nice way to start life at the dorm. Plus, I received a $20 CAD gift card for the campus food halls.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer:
Workday sucks, it just does. I had trouble with it because I am a graduate student, which meant I needed approval from individual lecturers to be admitted to the courses. It all worked out in the end, but it was quite stressful having only a few weeks before the semester started and not knowing whether I had secured the courses I wanted.
If possible, avoid graduate courses for this reason unless you know you have access to multiple faculties and therefore a wide range of courses to apply to. It worked out for me and for others, but be cautious. I had to choose graduate courses, so I did not have a choice.

Besides that the different intro videos gave an insight into some of the essentials. I don't think it's necessary to watch them while they are being streamed though. You get the same information out of scrolling through the slides. You just need to know which documents you need before entering Canada (ex. eta). You get acces to a canvas course where all that information is available.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
You have about a 50/50 chance of getting accommodation on campus. Even though you are prioritized as an exchange student, it is definitely not guaranteed.
If you are accepted, I believe they decide where to place you based on the prioritization list you created through the application platform.
There are two places where exchange students usually live on campus: Walter Gage, which is a tower where you live in apartments, and Fairview Crescent, where you live in a terraced house.
You live with roommates, often from other countries, and in Fairview it is usually with three, four, or five other roommates. You do have your own room.
Fairview is a bit cozier but farther from the main campus compared to Walter Gage, so I recommend looking into where you will have your courses. Either way, you will be within walking distance of everything on campus.
This year I would have preferred living at Fairview, but that is mostly because of the people. Another year it might have been different.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
Don't choose the meal plan! It's tailored for 1st year students (often 18 year olds), and it's therefore only available close to where they live. It's expensive as hell, you'll have to walk quite far when you have to eat, you can only eat when it's open and you have to sit there and consume your meal with other 18 year olds... 

Just go to No Frills once in a while in Kitsalano, that's what i did. Mealprepping will become a good solution to having to travel quite far for groceries. There is options on campus such as H-mart, Urban fare and Save on Foods, but they are all quite expensive compared to No Frills. Ironically Save on Foods is expensive, but the name is based on the fact that if you're a member you'll save quite a lot. If you choose to buy food often there, in the one thats in Westbrook village, i would highly recommend becomming a member. In general  a lot of stores will have membership deals. I recommend becoming a member. Create a new email if you dont want the spam.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Living on campus is not necessarily a better option socially. You dont choose your roomates, and i wasn't that lucky in that regard. I lived with some japanese students that barely knew english, so socializing and even talking about cleaning schedules were quite difficult.

It is however cheaper most times, and you'll live close to others that you might not live with, but that you meet through your time at UBC. It's therefore a safe option, and a cheap one, but living in the city can be nice if you find a good place and some nice roomates.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Fairview was really worn down. It was dirty, and there were a lot of rats. Honestly. But cheap.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Quite difficult as i mentioned previously. Workday is hard enough to navigate to begin with as an bachelor student, but even harder as a graduate student.

I sent out a lot of emails to instructors and admin personel, thats the only way forward as a grad student.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You get login information to workday, and navigate their platform.

When you plan for courses make sure they're available for that term.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
I was able to contact the Faculty of Forestry, they were quite helpful, but sometimes they took a long time to answer.

Go Global were also helpful, but they took forever to answer... Write everything in the first email you send to them.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got everything i wanted, but there is an add/drop period where you have time to get other courses, if the once you got initially isn't to your liking. Here you'll be able to add courses if others have dropped them and a spot has become available.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Choose undergrad courses.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I thought the course FRST 593 -  Climate adaption in socio ecological systems was a waste of time. It was a discussion based course, and we rarely touched on the relevant syllabus material. Often times personal anecdotes/stories from the teacher or students took up all of the time.

FRST 547 - Forestry in BC is a must in my opinion. Here you'll touch on some of the issues the province is facing in forestry, and you'll also get to go on 3 excursions!

FRST 509 - Advanced biometrics was interesting for me, as i haven't had statistics before. It's a bit harder, but doable if you put in the time.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I thought the courses were appropriate in how hard they were, some where however too easy. Forestry is however different in Canada, the nature is different and the issues they're facing are different. Therefore i wouldn't be too worried about picking 200, 300 or 400 level courses, as long as you've touched on the topics that is underlying for the course.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The grad courses were very down to earth, just as in Copenhagen. Distance between the lecturerer and students weren't big. The undergrad courses felt more like big highschool classes. I weren't allowed to take notes on my computer, because my lecturer felt young students couldn't administer it...

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
FRST 547 - Forestry in BC

FRST 593 - Climate Adaption in Socio-Ecological Systems

FRST 509 - Advanced Biometrics

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Read above.

But...

FRST 547 - Forestry in BC (Easy/moderate)

FRST 593 - Climate Adaption in Socio-Ecological Systems (EEEEEASY)

FRST 509 - Advanced Biometrics (moderate/hard)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I went on a lot of trips. They were expensive. You can do it on a way tighter budget, but i got carried away.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries were expensive, alcohol as well.

Eating out was a bit cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Sooo many clubs, use them!

My favorites: Surf club, Outdoor club, BJJ club, Wrestling club, Ski club

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
All the clubs, use them. There is so many i can't list them all.

The outdoor club is really popular, so you have to be really quick about getting on their trips. It's first come first serve, so look at their available trips often, they update them frequently.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to Whistler, Seattle and Vancouver Island.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Download Alltrails, a good app for looking up trails. Browse it and pick some beautiful areas.

Many times you'll have to rent a car. Do that through Evo or Turo!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy, Canadians are very easy going.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just go to club events. The surf trips were really fun. The same as with the outdoor clubs trips.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None really.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Their outdoor culture!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Use the weekends for trips!

Use the clubs.

Socialize early.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Looking at all the beautiful nature areas.

I had the chance of going to: Vancouver Island (4x), Interior BC, Whistler, Mount Rainier, Olympic National park, Yosemite, Yellowstone, Sequoia national park, Joshua Tree and many more.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The application process, and getting the courses.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
